overview: The Ilkhanate was the Mongol dynasty established by Hulagu in Iran and neighbouring lands, including Iraq, the southern Caucasus and much of Anatolia. The atlas’s broad outline runs from 1279 to 1400: it begins after the dynasty’s formation and continues long after central rule broke apart in 1335.

periods.title: Conquest and formation
periods.summary: Hulagu’s western campaigns prepared the regional dynasty.

periods.title: Regional Mongol rule
periods.summary: A dynasty ruled Iran and surrounding territories.

periods.title: Ghazan’s reign
periods.summary: Conversion, religious pressure and administrative reforms changed government.

periods.title: Royal and scholarly foundations
periods.summary: Monuments and illustrated manuscripts developed under courtly patronage.

periods.title: Fragmentation after Abu Said
periods.summary: Competing grandees supported rival claimants as central rule dissolved.

items.text: Hulagu’s army defeated most Iranian Ismaili strongholds in 1256 and captured Baghdad in 1258. The Abbasid caliph was executed. Soldiers had travelled west with families and herds, so the invasion also moved households into the region. Azerbaijan became an important centre of the new Mongol dynasty.

In 1294 the government tried paper money in Tabriz’s markets. The experiment failed amid financial disorder, livestock deaths and heavy court spending. For people buying food or selling goods, a ruler’s order could not by itself make an unfamiliar payment system work.

Ghazan adopted Islam in 1295, before securing the throne. Buddhist communities then faced forced conversion or departure, and temples, churches and synagogues suffered destruction. He later eased pressure on Christians and Jews. Religious policy changed within his reign and could have serious consequences for a family’s home and worship.

Ghazan’s government attempted regular tax schedules, land registration and tighter control over officials. Such changes mattered to farming families facing unpredictable demands. Much of the favourable account comes from his own minister Rashid al-Din, who helped implement the reforms; historians therefore treat claims of complete success cautiously.

sections.title: Schoolrooms, healthcare, food and essential work

items.text: Rashid al-Din’s 1309 endowment deed describes a Tabriz foundation with a classroom for orphans, a library, a hospital and a bath. It also funds teachers and students. One surviving document lets us look beyond a ruler’s throne into the places where people studied and received care.

The hospital’s planned staff included a doctor who taught as well as treated patients, an eye specialist who also performed surgery, and two trainee physicians. The trainees received pay and were to be replaced every five years. Learning medicine involved working alongside experienced practitioners.

The same foundation needed water carriers, cooks and sweepers. Its deed also assigned 220 enslaved men, with bread provisions for their wives; some cleaned water conduits or tended gardens. Public generosity depended partly on coerced labour, an uncomfortable part of how this institution functioned.

A soup kitchen was to feed one hundred poor people daily with bread and pottage. Workers counted the earthenware bowls afterward. Even a grand charitable institution had the familiar problem of keeping track of its dishes. This is a provision for one Tabriz complex, not every household’s menu.

At the Rab-e Rashidi dispensary, medicines were distributed on Mondays and Thursdays. A physician had to prescribe them; administration was supervised by the doctor or pharmacy staff. The rules reveal an organized service with designated responsibilities, rather than patients simply selecting an interesting-looking remedy from a shelf.

The endowment also supported copying scientific books to protect their contents from destruction. A paper mill, library and teaching institutions formed part of the complex described in UNESCO’s record. Preserving knowledge required materials, money and skilled hands: a handwritten backup took considerably more effort than pressing a button.

Construction of the Maragha observatory began in 1259, and it was operating by about 1261 or 1262. Nasir al-Din al-Tusi and colleagues investigated planetary motions as well as observing the sky. Their work questioned inherited astronomical models and developed mathematical alternatives, bringing critical argument into a major scholarly institution.

Al-Tusi also wrote about arithmetic using a board covered with dust, in a work apparently completed in 1264. A stylus could mark calculations, which were erased as the work proceeded. Dust offered a reusable surface, but erasing your steps made checking a mistake harder. Medieval mathematics could be wonderfully practical.

Ilkhanid workshops illustrated Rashid al-Din’s history and the Persian Book of Kings. In some royal images, ancient Iranian heroes wore clothing associated with Mongol rulers. These pictures were beautiful storytelling and political persuasion: the new ruling family could present itself within an older tradition of kingship.

Oljaytu’s mausoleum at Soltaniyeh, built in 1302 to 1312, has a dome about 50 metres high and eight slender minarets. Its turquoise exterior covers an ambitious double-shell structure, with inner and outer layers. The surviving building makes the builders’ skill in engineering, brickwork and decoration visible on an enormous scale.

A Kashan wall tile dated 1310 has raised blue letters, flowers and metallic-looking lustre over a white glaze. It combines moulding, painting and careful ceramic firing. The British Museum suggests its group may have decorated Isfahan’s Great Mosque, but that location remains a proposed connection rather than a secure excavation findspot.

sections.title: A dated piece of Arabic writing

items.text: On that tile, the Arabic phrase “wa kataba fī ghurrat shaʿbān” means “and written on the first day of Shaʿbān”. This is the museum’s Roman transcription of Arabic in thuluth script. The complete inscription dates the work to 1 Shaʿbān 709, identified by the catalogue as 4 January 1310: decoration that also keeps a calendar.

ending.text: Abu Said died in 1335 without a son to succeed him. Rival Mongol leaders backed different claimants, and the Ilkhanate fragmented. Political authority split among competing courts; the region’s people, scholarly traditions and crafts continued through those changes. The atlas’s 1400 endpoint is therefore not a historical date for the fall of a still-unified Ilkhanate.
